## Further Reading

Codesso, M., de Freitas, M. M., Wang, X., de Carvalho, A., & da Silva Filho, A. A. (2020). Continuous audit implementation at Cia. Hering in Brazil. *Journal of Emerging Technologies in Accounting*, *17*(2), 103–118. <https://doi.org/10.2308/jeta-2020-006> A case of internal auditors at a large Brazilian clothing company who implemented continuous auditing of the tax compliance of their manufacturing division by comparing the company's electronic invoices with data from the state tax office. It shows a monitoring test that compares internal records with an outside source, a kind of test this chapter's register does not include.

Gonzalez, G. C., & Hoffman, V. B. (2018). Continuous auditing's effectiveness as a fraud deterrent. *Auditing: A Journal of Practice & Theory*, *37*(2), 225–247. <https://doi.org/10.2308/ajpt-51828> An experiment on whether telling auditees promptly about the exceptions a monitoring system flags deters fraud. When the system's detection was weak, prompt notification increased participants' inclination to commit fraud, which is the reason this chapter keeps the monitoring report with internal audit.

Hardy, C. A., & Laslett, G. (2015). Continuous auditing and monitoring in practice: Lessons from Metcash's Business Assurance Group. *Journal of Information Systems*, *29*(2), 183–194. <https://doi.org/10.2308/isys-50969> A case study of an Australian distributor that runs more than a hundred automated tests every day, with an integrated system for managing their exceptions and visual reports for reviewing them. It describes the challenges of reaching that point and how the company distinguished continuous auditing from continuous monitoring.

Institute of Internal Auditors. (2025). *GTAG: Continuous auditing and monitoring* (3rd ed.). <https://www.theiia.org/en/content/guidance/recommended/supplemental/gtags/continuous-auditing-and-monitoring> The Institute of Internal Auditors' guidance on using technology to assess risks and controls on an ongoing basis, and on how continuous auditing works together with management's continuous monitoring. It is the professional companion to the research cited in this chapter.

Kobelsky, K. W. (2014). A conceptual model for segregation of duties: Integrating theory and practice for manual and IT-supported processes. *International Journal of Accounting Information Systems*, *15*(4), 304–322. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.accinf.2014.05.003> A model of which duties must be separated in manual and computer-supported processes. It adds the granting of access, and its authorization, to the duties that must be segregated, the reason the security table of Tutorial 16.3 is maintained by one person and approved by another.

Nickell, E. B., Schwebke, J. M., & Goldwater, P. M. (2023). An introductory audit data analytics case study: Using Microsoft Power BI and Benford's Law to detect accounting irregularities. *Journal of Accounting Education*, *64*, 100855. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jaccedu.2023.100855> A teaching case that builds a Benford's Law analysis in Power BI to look for irregularities in accounting data. It practices, on a different company, the anomaly test of Exercise 16.5.

Tronto, S., & Killingsworth, B. L. (2021). How internal audit can champion continuous monitoring in a business operation via visual reporting and overcome barriers to success. *The International Journal of Digital Accounting Research*, *21*, 23–59. <https://doi.org/10.4192/1577-8517-v21_2> An account of how a university's internal audit department worked with its procurement card program to build a continuous monitoring tool with visual reports, and of the barriers it met along the way. It shows internal audit helping management build monitoring that internal audit can then rely on.

Vasarhelyi, M. A., & Halper, F. B. (1991). The continuous audit of online systems. *Auditing: A Journal of Practice & Theory*, *10*(1), 110–125. <https://doi.org/10.2308/ajpt-9703192366> The paper that introduced continuous auditing, describing a system built for the internal auditors of AT&T Bell Laboratories that measured key figures of large systems, compared them with standards, and called the auditors' attention to problems. Much of the later research on continuous auditing starts from it.
